problem: Transformer VLN agents with explicit history (HAMT, E.T.) can only take local actions, so backtracking N steps requires N model calls. Prior topological-map VLN agents (EGP, SSM, GBE) do allow global actions, but they track state with recurrent memory and represent each node by a condensed visual feature, which is too coarse to ground the fine-grained object and room descriptions in goal-oriented instructions.
motivation: Goal-oriented VLN (REVERIE, SOON) gives high-level instructions such as 'water the plant on the table', so the agent must both explore efficiently and ground specific objects. An online topological map allows long-term planning over all observed navigable nodes, with shortest-path execution. But reasoning over a large graph pushes toward coarse node features, while grounding needs fine detail. The paper therefore reasons at two scales and fuses them dynamically.
key_idea: Build a topological map on the fly and choose the next goal among all map nodes by fusing two graph transformers: a coarse-scale one over pooled node features of the whole map (global actions) and a fine-scale one over image and object tokens at the current node (local actions and object grounding), weighted by a learned per-step gate.
insight: The two scales are complementary (Table 1, REVERIE val-unseen). The fine-only encoder stops well (SR/OSR 93.22) but explores poorly (OSR 30.96, SR 28.86). The coarse-only encoder explores well (OSR 46.44) but stops badly (SR/OSR 78.64, SR 36.52). Fusing them gives SR 45.81 with averaging and 46.98 with the dynamic gate; the gate's SPL gain over averaging is 1.79. Other ablations: graph-distance bias in self-attention (GASA) mainly helps efficiency (SPL 32.88→33.73, OSR 49.25→51.07). A DAgger-style pseudo interactive demonstrator beats RL fine-tuning (SR 46.98 vs 42.35). Speaker-synthesized instructions help pretraining but not policy fine-tuning. The learned gate weights the coarse scale most in mid-episode (0.36 at the start, 0.45 in the middle, 0.42 at the end), when exploration and backtracking matter. The agent backtracks in 48.6% of val-unseen trajectories vs 13.7% in val-seen.
method: Topological mapping: at each step, add the current node and its unvisited neighbours to the graph. Encode the panorama's image and object tokens with a 2-layer transformer. The current-node feature is the average of these tokens. Each navigable (unvisited) node's feature is the average of the view embeddings from which it was seen.
Text encoder: 9-layer transformer (LXMERT-initialized) over word, position and type embeddings.

Coarse-scale cross-modal encoder: 4 layers over all map nodes plus a 'stop' node. Node inputs add an egocentric location encoding (orientation and distance to the current node) and a last-visited-step encoding. Each layer is cross-attention to text followed by graph-aware self-attention, which adds a learned bias M = E·W_e + b_e from the pairwise graph-distance matrix. An FFN scores every node; visited nodes are masked.

Fine-scale cross-modal encoder: 4-layer LXMERT-style cross-modal transformer over [stop token r0; panorama views; objects] at the current node. Inputs carry the node's position relative to the start plus each neighbour's relative position. It scores local actions and, via an FFN, target objects for grounding.

Dynamic fusion: map local scores into the global action space; every non-neighbour node gets the summed score of visited neighbours as a backtrack score. Compute σ_t = Sigmoid(FFN([v̂0; r̂0])) and final score s_i = σ_t·s^c_i + (1−σ_t)·s^f'_i. The chosen node is reached via Floyd shortest path on the built map. If the step budget runs out, the agent returns to the node with the highest stop probability.

Training: pretraining with SAP (behaviour cloning), OG, MLM and MRC. The policy is then fine-tuned with a pseudo interactive demonstrator (DAgger-like): it uses the GT graph to pick the navigable node minimizing distance from the current node plus distance to the goal. Loss L = λ·L_SAP + L_PID + L_OG, with λ = 0.2.

setting.backbone: LXMERT-initialized multi-layer transformers (text 9 / panorama 2 / coarse 4 / fine 4 layers, hidden 768) over frozen ImageNet ViT-B/16 image features (ViT features for REVIERE boxes; BUTD detector for SOON objects); fine-tuned
setting.training_data: REVERIE: train split (10,466 instr.) plus 19,636 speaker-synthesized instructions in pretraining (30,102 pairs), then PID fine-tuning on original data. SOON: train split (2,780 instr.) with automatically cleaned BUTD boxes, no augmentation. R2R: train plus PREVALENT augmented data in pretraining.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (view features with orientations) + object features (REVERIE-annotated boxes or BUTD detections) + node GPS coordinates / neighbour positions
setting.action_space: global: any navigable node in the online topological map (discrete Matterport3D nav-graph viewpoints) or stop, executed by shortest path over the map; plus object selection at the stop location
setting.privileged: none beyond the standard discrete VLN setting (nav-graph neighbour connectivity and node coordinates); REVERIE uses the benchmark-provided candidate object boxes. GT graph is used only for the training demonstrator.

numbers_note: R2R results are printed as integers (SR/SPL). SOON results use the released challenge split rather than the original paper's split, and SOON grounding success is judged by the predicted object centre lying inside the annotated polygon. Additional REVERIE val-unseen ablations are not listed: average fusion, GASA on/off, augmentation during PID, and λ sweep (λ=0 gives SR 48.22, SPL 33.00). An R4R row appears in the dataset statistics table but no R4R results are reported in the given text.
results: On REVERIE test-unseen, DUET reaches SR 52.51 / SPL 36.06 / RGSPL 22.06, beating HAMT (30.40 / 26.67 / 13.08) by 22.11 SR, 9.39 SPL and 8.98 RGSPL. On val-unseen it reaches SR 46.98 vs HAMT 32.95. On SOON test-unseen it gets SR 33.44 / SPL 21.42 vs GBE 12.90 / 9.23. On R2R it raises SR to 72 (val-unseen) and 69 (test-unseen), vs 66 and 65 for HAMT-e2e. SPL is only comparable (60 vs 61; 59 vs 60) because backtracking lengthens trajectories. Even DUET-coarse (SR 68 / 67) beats prior map-based methods (SSM 62 / 61).
limitations: Restricted to discrete nav-graph environments: relies on known neighbour connectivity and node coordinates, and global actions are executed by teleport-like shortest-path moves.
Large seen/unseen gap. Backtracking-heavy exploration raises trajectory length, so R2R SPL does not improve. SOON performance stays low (RGSPL ~4) given its small training set.
Fine-grained scene and object grounding remains a failure mode: 29.82% of REVERIE stops are in the wrong room type. Predictions are also not robust across paraphrased instructions.
